promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Reflection on the methods of the historian

questions.q: The historical investigation (IA) has three sections: evaluation of sources, the investigation and:
questions.explain: The IA comprises source evaluation, the investigation, and a reflection on historical methods.

questions.q: In the source-evaluation section, two sources are assessed using:
questions.explain: Students evaluate two sources' OPVL in relation to the investigation.

questions.q: The investigation section should:
options: Present a structured, evidence-based analysis answering the research question
List random facts with no argument
questions.explain: A strong investigation builds a reasoned, evidenced argument addressing the question.

questions.q: The reflection considers:
options: The methods and challenges faced by historians
questions.explain: Reflection links the student's experience to the wider methods and limitations of the historian.

questions.q: A good historical research question is:
options: Focused, historical and answerable with evidence
questions.explain: Effective questions are narrow enough to answer with available evidence.

questions.q: A primary source differs from a secondary source in that a primary source is:
options: From the time of the events
Always written by a historian later
questions.explain: Primary sources originate from the period studied; secondary sources interpret it afterwards.

questions.q: In OPVL, the 'purpose' of a source refers to:
options: Why it was created and for whom
questions.explain: Purpose examines the author's intention and audience.

questions.q: The reliability of a source is best judged by considering:
options: Its origin and purpose, and corroboration with other sources
questions.explain: Reliability depends on provenance and how far other evidence supports it.

questions.q: A challenge historians commonly face is:
options: Bias, gaps in evidence and the need to select sources
questions.explain: Historians work with incomplete, biased and selected evidence.

questions.q: Cross-referencing (corroboration) means:
questions.explain: Corroboration tests whether different sources support the same conclusions.

questions.q: A limitation of relying on official government documents is that they:
options: May present an official or biased viewpoint
questions.explain: Official records can reflect the state's perspective and omit other voices.

questions.q: The historical concept of 'significance' asks:
options: Why an event or person mattered
questions.explain: Significance evaluates the importance and impact of events, people or developments.

questions.q: In history, establishing causation means showing that:
options: One factor helped bring about another
questions.explain: Causation links causes to outcomes, going beyond mere correlation or sequence.

questions.q: An 'anachronism' in historical writing is:
options: Judging the past by present-day standards or misplacing it in time
questions.explain: Historians avoid anachronism by understanding the past on its own terms.

questions.q: The particular value of an eyewitness account is that it offers:
options: A first-hand perspective, though memory and bias are limitations
questions.explain: Eyewitnesses provide immediacy but can be affected by bias and memory.

questions.q: To reduce bias in an investigation, a historian should:
options: Use a range of sources and perspectives
Choose only sources they agree with
questions.explain: Consulting varied, corroborating perspectives limits the impact of any one bias.

questions.q: The 'provenance' of a source refers to its:
questions.explain: Provenance is the source's origin, including who made it and when.

questions.q: A key point of the reflection is that historians:
options: Interpret incomplete evidence and cannot be wholly objective
questions.explain: History involves interpretation of partial, imperfect evidence.

questions.q: Deciding which sources to include and which to leave out is an example of:
options: Selection, a method and challenge of the historian
questions.explain: Selection of evidence is a deliberate, reflective part of historical method.

questions.q: A hypothesis in a historical investigation is:
options: A proposed answer tested against the evidence
A proven fact needing no evidence
questions.explain: A hypothesis is a tentative claim evaluated using the gathered evidence.

specSource: IB Diploma History guide (first assessment 2020); Historical investigation (internal assessment)
